prompt.context: The CEO of a major Swiss insurance company approached the CEO of our client, another major Swiss insurance company, about the possibility of merging.
prompt.question: How would you determine if this is a good idea?

clarifying_info.q: What lines of business do both companies operate in?
clarifying_info.a: The main business for both is property casualty insurance (car and home insurance). Ignore other areas such as life insurance for this case.
They both cover the same geographic area: Switzerland only.

clarifying_info.q: What is their combined market share?
clarifying_info.a: Together the two firms hold 23% of the market. The rest of the market is fragmented.

clarifying_info.q: How do they sell their insurance?
clarifying_info.a: Both companies sell insurance through company-employed agents, as opposed to independent brokers.

framework: Assess strategic fit: similarities in business lines, customer base, geography, and distribution channel
Identify cost synergies: overhead reduction (actuaries, executives, advertising, HQ, regulatory compliance, agents, IT systems)
Quantify claims savings: use increased market power to negotiate lower reimbursement rates with repair shops
Assess revenue impact: evaluate whether combined scale drives pricing power or if commodity nature limits upside
Evaluate risks: potential revenue loss from agent cuts, regulatory scrutiny given combined market share, customer/pricing transparency issues
Recommend: weigh total synergy value against integration costs and risks

questions.prompt: What are the pros and cons you would expect with the merger? Start with the pros (cost reduction side).
questions.guidance: Strong answers focus on: (1) overhead savings — fewer actuaries, executives, advertising spend, headquarters, regulatory compliance teams; (2) distribution savings — fewer company-employed agents needed where there is geographic overlap; (3) claims cost reduction — use combined market power to set maximum reimbursement rates (similar to HMO rate-setting) and negotiate preferred deals with garages and mechanics.

questions.prompt: You mentioned using market power to reduce the amount paid on claims. How much are claims and how much could be saved?
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate claims as a share of revenue using car insurance economics: average car value ~$20,000, repairs ~5% of value = ~$1,000 in expected claims per car per year, average premium ~$1,200/year, so profit ~$200/car, meaning claims are roughly 83-85% of revenue. The candidate should then apply the 5% savings rate to the combined claims base.

math.setup: Each company pays $700M in claims annually. Combined claims = $700M x 2 = $1.4B. Apply 5% savings from market power.

questions.prompt: What would be the savings in overhead efficiencies — for example, how many fewer agents would you need, and what would that depend on?
questions.guidance: Savings depend on geographic overlap and whether agents are currently working at capacity. With exact duplication, savings could be up to 50% of one company's agent headcount (though that is probably not realistic). Key risk: cutting too many agents could hurt sales. Other overhead areas: call centers, billing and mailing systems, duplicate IT forms and platforms.

questions.prompt: How would the revenue side be affected by the merger?
questions.guidance: The combined market share is still only 23% in a fragmented market, so competitive pricing pressure remains. Property/casualty insurance is a commodity product; revenue should not be expected to increase materially beyond simply combining the two firms' existing revenues. Candidate should also note that using market power to reduce claims payouts is effectively a price hike on customers — this may face regulatory scrutiny or customer backlash if the market is transparent enough.

brainstorming.prompt: What overhead efficiencies could be achieved by merging the two insurance companies?

categories.name: Infrastructure / IT
ideas: Eliminate duplicate IT platforms and forms

categories.name: Marketing / Brand
ideas: Single advertising spend instead of two competing budgets

categories.name: Real Estate / HQ
ideas: Reduce office footprint in overlapping locations

recommendation: Because the two firms are highly similar — same business lines, same customer base, same geography, same distribution model — there are significant efficiencies to be gained in overhead reduction
Increased combined market power will allow the merged entity to cut claims costs, estimated at $70M annually from a 5% reduction on $1.4B in combined claims
risks: Cutting too many company-employed agents could hurt revenue if sales capacity drops
Reducing claim reimbursement rates is effectively a price increase; this may face regulatory scrutiny or customer pushback in a transparent market
Integration complexity and one-time merger costs could offset near-term savings
next_steps: Conduct detailed overlap analysis of agent territories to determine safe headcount reduction levels
Model full synergy case including all overhead categories with conservative and aggressive scenarios
Engage regulatory advisors early to assess antitrust and pricing-regulation risk in Switzerland
